title: LeCun and Balestriero say two views of one scene beat a bigger language model
friendlyTitle: Yann LeCun and a co-author say two views of one scene beat a bigger language model
summary: In a paper submitted on 29 October, Randall Balestriero and Yann LeCun argue that joint-embedding models trained separately on different kinds of data learn the same representation, up to one rotation, when each training pair is two observations of one scene. They call next-token prediction a poor version of that setup, because it pairs pieces of one document rather than two views of one thing. On their tests, those paired views needed 42 times fewer samples than next-token prediction to reach the same alignment. A 109-million-parameter text model aligned with image encoders better than the language models they tried, up to 72 billion parameters.
friendlySummary: In a paper submitted on 29 October, Randall Balestriero and Yann LeCun argue that models trained separately on different kinds of data can learn the same picture of the world, up to one rotation, when each training pair is two observations of one scene. They say ordinary language-model training is a weak version of that, because it pairs pieces of one document rather than two views of one thing. On their tests, those paired views needed 42 times fewer examples than ordinary training to line up as well. A text model with 109 million parameters lined up with image models better than the language models they tried, including ones up to 72 billion parameters.
whyItMatters: This is a paper, not a switch in a product you use today. The practical claim is about training, not about chat quality: pairing two views of the same thing can matter more than making the model larger. If you are choosing or training models that have to share a picture of the world, the abstract is the claim to test, not a result to treat as settled.
